newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.LANKA STRIVING TO BECOME REGION'S FINANCIAL HUB.
newsitem.headline: S.LANKA STRIVING TO BECOME REGION'S FINANCIAL HUB.

text.p: Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga said on Monday her government would implement policies to ensure that the country became a leading financial centre in Asia.

"The government is committed to making Colombo the major financial centre not only in South Asia but the whole of Asia," Kumaratunga said while inaugurating the Colombo Stock Exchange's fully automated trading system.
"The government will progressively adopt policies intended to move towards this goal," added Kumaratunga, who is also finance minister.

Rienzie Wijetilleke, chairman of the exchange, said the perennial problem of low liquidity was one of the main areas which needed to be addressed if the bourse was to become competitive and attract foreign capital.

He said Sri Lankan investors should be allowed to invest abroad, overseas companies should be permitted to list and trade in foreign exchange and firms which go public should be given tax concessions.
Government-run pension funds, gratuity funds and banks should also be encouraged to invest in the market, Wijetilleke said.
"The Employees' Provident Fund, the Employees Trust Fund, Sri Lanka Insurance Company and the National Savings Bank, should be encouraged to invest on the stock exchange...," he said.

The positive sentiment on the stock exchange, which has seen the all share price index rise some 250 points between January and June 1997, was possible only due to vigorous financial reforms and strict monetary policy controls, said deputy finance minister Gamini Peiris.
"The government was able to take steps to cut money supply to about 11 percent in June 1977 from around 19 percent in November 1996," he said.
"This led to a three percent cut in reserve ratios of commercial banks, which in turn resulted in lower interest rates."
